lens: E, the baseline code (src/submeter, tests, scripts/platform_check.py, pyproject.toml)

findings.title: A gap batch counts as covered time with zero use, so means, percentiles and coverage come out wrong
findings.evidence: uv run python docs/review/probes/e-baseline/rollup_cases.py (real Sampler, Attributor, RawFile, roll_up and merge; 2 cores busy, one hour of sleep): 'minute bucket at +90 min: covered_s=3601 of width 60, cpu_s=0, p50 cores=0.005, well_covered=True'; 'three hours merged: covered_s=10800 (awake for 7200), cpu_s=14398, mean cores over covered time=1.33, p25=0.007, p50=1.951 (the workload used 2.00 cores whenever it was observed)'. Chain: sampler.py:59 gives a gap batch interval_s=max(elapsed, wall); rules.py:221 copies batch.interval_s into each WorkloadSample, which has no gap field (models.py:135-147); raw.py:112-129 stores it; rollup.py:53,60,70-71 add it to covered_s and weight mean memory and both histograms by it. docs/06-storage.md:38 says covered seconds exist 'so a gap is never read as zero use'.
findings.impact: After any sleep, a workload's minute bucket claims 3600 s covered in a 60 s bucket, hourly means and p50/p25 drop toward zero, and well_covered() passes. Baselines, trends and the verdict read sleep as idle use.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/collector/sampler.py: a gap batch keeps interval_s = monotonic elapsed (or 0) and reports the gap span separately. core/models.py: add gap: bool to WorkloadSample. attribution/rules.py aggregate: pass the flag through. store/rollup.py SeriesAccumulator.add: skip gap samples. store/raw.py write: for a gap batch write the gap row and no workload rows. Add one test that rolls up across a gap.
findings.cost: About 15 changed lines in four modules plus one test
findings.refutation_attempt: Searched docs/05, docs/06 and docs/17 for a rule that gap samples are excluded from rollups: only the general statement exists. Re-read the rollup path for a filter on interval_s or gap: none. The probe drives the real pipeline end to end, not a copy.
findings.related_prior_findings: R08, R24 (the fix is not applied in the baseline); lead reviewer's lead 2

findings.title: Workload memory is a sum of per-process RSS, overstating multi-process workloads by 1.4 to 5 times
findings.evidence: uv run python docs/review/probes/e-baseline/memory_sum.py (the signed-in user's own processes grouped by name, as an exe rule would): 'chrome 17 processes: summed RSS 3115 MiB, PSS 1599, USS 1369, x1.95'; 'claude 10: 3474 / 2475 / 2353, x1.40'; 'Web Content 3: 223 / 43 / 23, x5.14'; 'all 155 own processes: RSS 11327 MiB, PSS 6659 MiB, x1.70'. Code: psutil_provider.py:63 sets memory_bytes = private (Windows) or rss (elsewhere); rules.py:207 sums it per workload; cli.py:101 prints it. docs/06-storage.md:83 says workload totals use 'USS or PSS'. ProcessCounters has one memory field (models.py:82), so the growth unit and the totals unit cannot both be carried.
findings.impact: The memory column of submeter top and the memory_bytes stored in workload_raw are wrong on Linux by the shared pages counted once per process. On Windows, private bytes do not double-count sharing but are commit, not resident USS, so the figure is a different quantity from the one the brief names.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/core/models.py: split memory into memory_growth_bytes (private bytes, or RSS plus swap) and memory_total_bytes: int | None with the time it was read; aggregate sums only memory_total_bytes and marks the workload partial when some members lack it; cli top labels the figure. docs/06 and docs/08 state what a workload total shows when USS/PSS is known only for the uss_top_n largest processes.
findings.cost: About 20 lines in models, provider and aggregate now; after the build starts, every provider, the raw schema and every reader
findings.decision_question: When USS/PSS is read only for the 25 largest processes (uss_top_n), what is a workload's memory total? Options: (a) show it as partial, with the count of processes measured; (b) read PSS for every readable process at the cold interval on Linux (smaps_rollup), and USS for the top N on Windows; (c) show private bytes and label them as such. Recommendation: (a) now, then measure the cost of (b).
findings.refutation_attempt: docs/14 says 'Memory is private bytes on Windows and resident memory elsewhere', which names the unit but not that it is summed as the workload total. R06 chose private bytes for leak detection, not for totals. Checked for a second memory field in any record: none.

findings.title: Records cannot say 'unavailable': unreadable I/O is summed as zero and labelled polled, and one failed call zeroes CPU and memory
findings.evidence: docs/review/probes/e-baseline/attribution_cases.out.txt: 'process dockerd: io_read_bytes=None' then 'workload docker: source=polled, io_read_bytes=0, io_write_bytes=0'. interface_cases.out.txt: 'ProcessCounters with cpu_s=None: refused', 'memory_bytes=None: refused', 'WorkloadSample with io_read_bytes=None: refused'. provider_cases.out.txt (psutil patched to deny one call): 'num_threads started=1000 cpu_s=0 memory_MiB=0 threads=0 ... restricted=True'; on this machine '457 processes, 299 restricted; of the restricted: 299 lack I/O counters, 0 lack a command line, 0 lack a start time, ... 187 have CPU time above zero'. Code: models.py:79,82 and 142-145 are required numbers; psutil_provider.py:58-66 reads CPU, memory and threads in one try and sets zeros; rules.py:208-209 adds None as 0; rules.py:216 labels everything but the Restricted bucket POLLED; raw.py:43-44 io columns NOT NULL. AGENTS.md: 'A metric the system cannot deliver is reported as unavailable, never as zero'.
findings.impact: Any rule that matches another user's process (dockerd, a service) shows 0 bytes of I/O as a measured figure. The one restricted flag means 'I/O unreadable' for two thirds of processes on Linux, so the Restricted bucket and the capability note ('299 of 457 not fully readable') describe processes whose CPU and memory are exact.
findings.proposed_change: core/models.py: cpu_s, memory and I/O fields become Optional (None = unavailable) in ProcessCounters, ProcessSample and WorkloadSample, and WorkloadSample gains a count of members with a field missing; drop or narrow restricted to 'CPU or memory unreadable'. providers/psutil_provider.py: read each field in its own try. attribution/rules.py aggregate: a workload field is None (or partial with the count) when any member's is None, and its source is PARTIAL. store/raw.py: those columns nullable.
findings.cost: About 40 lines now; later every provider, store, rollup and reader
findings.decision_question: When some processes in a workload have a field unavailable, is the workload figure (a) unavailable, or (b) the sum of the readable ones plus a count of unreadable members, labelled partial? Recommendation: (b), since it keeps the readable part and states the gap, as docs/17 says for the Restricted bucket ('with whatever is visible').
findings.refutation_attempt: Looked for a place that turns None into 'unavailable' later (store, cli): none; WorkloadSample cannot hold None at all. Checked whether the 299 restricted processes on Linux are restricted for CPU: 0 lack a start time and 187 have CPU above zero, so CPU is readable and only I/O is missing.

findings.title: On Windows the System Idle Process (pid 0) will likely be read as a process holding all idle CPU time
findings.evidence: psutil C, psutil_handle_from_pid (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/giampaolo/psutil/master/psutil/arch/windows/proc_utils.c): 'if (pid == 0) { // otherwise we'd get NoSuchProcess return psutil_oserror_ad("automatically set for PID 0"); }'. .venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/psutil/_pswindows.py:938-947: cpu_times() on a permission error falls back to self._proc_info() and returns its user_time and kernel_time; psutil proc.c psutil_proc_oneshot computes those from the SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION entry with a pid 0 case only for create_time. Microsoft Learn, Windows Internals 6E excerpt (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/blogs/microsoft_press/christophe-nasarre-excerpt-2-from-windows-internals-6e): 'Idle process (contains one thread per CPU to account for idle CPU time)'. psutil_provider.py:54-110 reads pid 0 like any process (the fallback succeeds, so it is not even restricted); rules.py:156 puts it in Unattributed; the SYSTEM name (rules.py:36) is defined and never assigned anywhere in src/.
findings.impact: On an idle 8-core machine, Unattributed would show about 7.9 cores, process CPU would exceed the machine's busy time, the reconciliation rule (R07) fails and unattributed_alert fires all the time. platform_check.py has no check that would notice.
findings.proposed_change: docs/05-data-flow.md and providers/base.py: providers exclude pid 0 (idle comes from system counters) and map pid 4 System, Registry, MemCompression and Secure System to the SYSTEM bucket. scripts/platform_check.py: add a check that the summed per-process CPU delta over 5 s does not exceed the machine busy delta by more than 5%.
findings.cost: A few lines in the provider and attribution, one check in platform_check.py
findings.refutation_attempt: Searched docs/ and scripts/ for 'idle process', 'pid 0' and 'System Idle': nothing. Checked psutil for a special case that skips pid 0 in process_iter or zeroes its times: the only pid 0 cases are name() and create_time. Not marked verified because the idle entry's times have not been read on Windows.
findings.would_confirm: On Windows: uv run python -c "import psutil,time;p=psutil.Process(0);a=sum(p.cpu_times()[:2]);time.sleep(5);print(sum(p.cpu_times()[:2])-a, psutil.cpu_count())" (about 5 x idle cores confirms), then uv run submeter top --json on an idle machine and look for an unattributed total of several cores

findings.title: The brief's 'recover reaped children's CPU from the parent's child-time counters' double-counts any child that was seen alive
findings.evidence: uv run python docs/review/probes/e-baseline/children_time.py (Linux, real processes): '1. A child seen alive ... last seen alive with 0.42 CPU-s; the parent's child time then rose by 0.42 CPU-s; crediting both gives 0.84 for 0.42 used'; '2. A grandchild whose parent exits first: the grandchild used 0.31 CPU-s; this process's child time rose by 0.05 CPU-s (the launcher's own start-up only)'. docs/17-build-prompt.md:71: 'On Linux, recover reaped children's CPU time from the parent's child-time counters.' psutil_provider.py:62 uses user+system only and ProcessCounters (models.py:71-84) has no child-time field.
findings.impact: Built as written, every polled child that was sampled before exiting is counted twice, inventing CPU for exactly the spawn-heavy agent workloads. Orphaned grandchildren (common with shells and daemons) are not recovered at all, so the recovery also cannot close the gap it is meant to close.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md: 'Credit a parent's child-time delta minus the last-seen cumulative CPU of its children that exited in the interval. Orphans reaped by a subreaper or by init are not recovered.' core/models.py: add children_cpu_s: float | None to ProcessCounters now, so the /proc reader and the sampler do not both have to change the shared record later.
findings.cost: Two sentences in docs/17, one field in models.py
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked docs/05, docs/10 and R01 for a rule on double counting or subtraction: none. Ran the child case with the parent reaping, as a shell or build tool does; the full 0.42 s lands in the parent's counter.

findings.title: The fixed 30-second gap rule turns intervals the settings allow into gaps, and top --seconds 31 to 60 prints zeros
findings.evidence: sampler_cases.out.txt: 'idle_interval 60s: gap=True, used 30 CPU-s, credited 0'; 'idle_interval 5s x on_battery_multiplier 10: gap=True, used 25 CPU-s, credited 0'; 'idle_interval 20s x on_battery_multiplier 2: gap=True'. cli_cases.out.txt: 'top --seconds 31: exit code 0, interval_s=31.1, CPU-seconds summed over all workloads=0.000' (and --seconds 2 gives 3.510). Code: sampler.py:39 gap_after_s=30.0, sampler.py:55; config.py:46-51 idle and cold up to 60s, config.py:92 battery multiplier up to 10; cli.py:79 allows up to 60.
findings.impact: A valid idle or battery cadence records every interval as unobserved, so the machine looks unmeasured whenever it is quiet or on battery, and the documented top command silently prints all zeros.
findings.proposed_change: collector/sampler.py: ingest takes the expected interval for this tick and calls it a gap only when monotonic elapsed exceeds a multiple of it (or wall minus monotonic exceeds the slack); cli.py top: pass gap_after_s above --seconds. docs/14 entry for the sampler updated.
findings.cost: About 6 lines and one test
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked whether the collector loop is meant to construct Sampler with a larger gap_after_s: docs/14 and docs/17 state 'an interval longer than 30 seconds ... is a gap' as fixed behaviour, and nothing ties it to the configured intervals.

findings.title: The sampler assumes every snapshot holds every process, so the hot and cold sets lose cold CPU and invent exits and starts
findings.evidence: sampler_cases.out.txt case 2 (hot every 1 s, cold every 10 s, 20 s): 'hot process used 18.00 CPU-s, credited 18.00; 30 cold processes used 2.40 CPU-s, credited 0.00; 60 exits and 60 starts were reported, and none happened'. Case 7 (a live process missing from one snapshot): 'used 4.8 CPU-s over 6 s and was credited 3.2; 1 exit and 1 start were reported'. Code: sampler.py:49 replaces the known set with the latest snapshot only; sampler.py:65 calls everything absent 'exited'; models.py:126 one interval_s for all processes. docs/17-build-prompt.md:71 requires hot and cold sets.
findings.impact: Cold processes (90% of them by docs/08's formula) lose their CPU, every cold read counts them as newly started, the raw store finishes and re-registers them, and the started counter (a cost metric) is inflated.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md and docs/05: state that the bulk read returns cumulative counters for every process every tick and the hot and cold sets only gate expensive extras (USS, handles, working folder); or else Snapshot gains complete: bool and ProcessSample its own interval_s, and the Sampler keeps the last counters of processes absent from a partial snapshot.
findings.cost: One paragraph in the brief (option a) or about 25 lines in sampler and models (option b)
findings.decision_question: Do hot and cold sets decide (a) which expensive extras are read, with CPU, memory and I/O read for every process every tick, or (b) which processes appear in a snapshot at all? Recommendation: (a). The Windows bulk call returns every process anyway, and (a) keeps one interval per batch.
findings.refutation_attempt: Looked in docs/05 and docs/17 for which fields the cold set skips: not stated. The sampler has no parameter for a partial snapshot.

findings.title: A counter that was a stand-in zero becomes the baseline, so a process readable again is credited its whole lifetime of CPU
findings.evidence: sampler_cases.out.txt case 1 (restricted with cpu_s=0, then readable at 5000): 'interval 1 s, gap=False, first_seen=False: credited 5000 CPU-s to a 1-second interval'. Case 4 (start time unreadable, then readable): 'exited=[9], first_seen=True, credited 0 CPU-s: one process is recorded as an exit and a start'. Code: sampler.py:80-81 subtracts before.cpu_s with no check of before.restricted and no upper bound; psutil_provider.py:66 writes 0.0 on AccessDenied; psutil_provider.py:102-110 writes started=0.0.
findings.impact: One flip invents thousands of CPU-seconds in one interval for one workload. How often psutil 7.2.2 produces the flip is unknown: on Windows cpu_times and memory_info fall back to NtQuerySystemInformation (_pswindows.py:789-811, 938-947), so a future bulk or /proc provider is the more likely source.
findings.proposed_change: collector/sampler.py: if the earlier record was unreadable for a field, treat that field as having no baseline (credit 0, as for an old first sighting); cap every per-process CPU delta at interval x logical_cores and count capped samples. providers: never fabricate started=0.0 (the key needs a real start or the process is reported without one).
findings.cost: About 8 lines and two tests
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked the sampler for a sanity cap or a restricted check: none. Checked psutil for when the zero path triggers: rarely with psutil, which is why the frequency is marked unknown, but the Sampler contract accepts any provider.

findings.title: An inherited workload is lost when the parent exits, and the raw process table keeps the first workload forever
findings.evidence: attribution_cases.out.txt: 'reparented to pid 1: pid 12 was agent:untagged (inherited from pid 11), then unattributed (no rule matched); totals after: {unattributed: 2.0, agent:untagged: 0.1}', the same with the parent pid left stale, and 'a server the agent started: agent:untagged while the agent runs, then unattributed'. raw_store_cases.out.txt: process table '[(sh, sh run-node, unattributed, 9.1)]' while 'workload_raw totals: [(builds, 9.0), (unattributed, 0.1)]'. Code: rules.py:130-163 rebuilds every attribution from the current batch alone; raw.py:132-133 and 158-169 register a process once with INSERT OR IGNORE.
findings.impact: Agent children that outlive an intermediate shell, and background servers, move to Unattributed mid-run, which is the attribution job failing for agent workloads. Per-process history disagrees with the workload totals.
findings.proposed_change: attribution/rules.py: Attributor keeps a ProcessKey to Attribution map across batches; an attribution sticks until the process exits, and rules are re-tried only when exe or cmdline changes. store/raw.py: record a workload change (a workload column in process_raw, or a process_workload table with a start time).
findings.cost: About 20 lines plus a test
findings.decision_question: When a process execs into a program that a different rule matches, does it (a) keep its inherited workload, or (b) move to the rule's workload? Recommendation: keep inheritance sticky, and let an explicit rule match win, recording the change.
findings.refutation_attempt: docs/17 says a parent link counts only if the parent started first; nothing says what happens when the parent goes. Checked RawFile for an update path: none.

findings.title: aggregate() labels a polled sum as 'kernel', and the test asserts that label
findings.evidence: attribution_cases.out.txt: 'source=kernel, cpu_s=0.4: the label says kernel, the figure is the polled sum. aggregate() has no parameter that carries a group's own totals'. Code: rules.py:196-216 (kernel_workloads only changes the label); tests/test_baseline.py:268-272 asserts source 'kernel' for a polled sum.
findings.impact: A builder who wires the launcher by passing kernel_workloads gets the polled undercount shown as exact kernel accounting, which is the R01 problem with a label that hides it.
findings.proposed_change: attribution/rules.py aggregate: take group totals (a mapping from workload to the group's cumulative CPU, I/O and process counts) and use them for KERNEL workloads, keeping the polled sum only as a cross-check; refuse kernel_workloads without totals. tests/test_baseline.py:268-272: assert the group's figure, not the label.
findings.cost: About 15 lines and one test change
findings.refutation_attempt: Looked for another path that replaces a kernel workload's figures: none in src/. docs/14 says aggregate 'marks each workload as measured by the kernel', which is only the label.

findings.title: ProcessKey.started is a wall-clock float that differs between providers and after a clock step
findings.evidence: interface_cases.out.txt: 'psutil equals ticks/100 + btime: True; with boot time taken from the two clocks instead of btime the value differs by 0.925 s ... same pid, same process, unequal keys: True'. provider_cases.out.txt (boot time patched to simulate a 1 h step back): 'its child, born after the step, has a start time -3599 s from its parent's, and is attributed to unattributed'. psutil/__init__.py:776-781: create_time 'is based on the system clock, which means it may be affected by changes such as manual adjustments or time synchronization (e.g. NTP)'. models.py:68 started: float; raw.py:38,47 REAL primary keys.
findings.impact: When the bulk provider falls back to psutil (R17), or the /proc reader computes boot time differently, every process gets a new key: all report as exited and started, the interval's CPU of older processes is credited 0, and the process table is duplicated. After a clock step, parent links fail and new children are credited no CPU.
findings.proposed_change: core/models.py: ProcessKey.started becomes the platform's integer start stamp (Linux: starttime ticks since boot from /proc/PID/stat field 22, with the boot id; Windows: CreateTime as a FILETIME integer), with a separate wall-clock time for display. store/raw.py: INTEGER columns. docs/05: say which stamp every provider must produce.
findings.cost: Small now; after the build, a raw schema migration and three providers
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked whether psutil's cache keeps keys stable: it does for an existing Process object, but not across providers or for processes born after a step. Checked psutil pid reuse: its ppid() call runs is_running(), so a reused pid is dropped for one snapshot rather than mis-keyed (see nothing_found).

findings.title: The leak gate sits on the threshold, and a decimal 50 MB per hour is never flagged
findings.evidence: uv run python docs/review/probes/e-baseline/growth_cases.py (check_growth at the defaults, one point a minute, 20 seeds): 'leak 50 MB/h, noise +/-2 MB: 9 flagged within 125 min, 19 flagged at all ... 1 never'; 'leak 47.6837 MB/h [50,000,000 bytes an hour], noise +/-0 MB: 0 flagged ... 20 never (growth is below the threshold)'; 'an 80 MB/h leak ... 120 minute buckets (two hours of data): flagged=False, reason=not enough data yet, duration_s=7140'; 55 MB/h: 20 of 20 within 125 min. Code: growth.py:72-78; config.py:121 min_slope 50 MiB/h (units.py:29-35 binary). docs/01-overview.md:18: 'A leak of 50 MB an hour is flagged within 2 hours'.
findings.impact: The acceptance gate passes or fails by chance at 50 MiB/h, and fails every time if the load generator leaks decimal megabytes. Two hours of minute buckets span 119 minutes, so a flag at exactly 2 hours is impossible.
findings.proposed_change: docs/01-overview.md:18 and the gate in docs/15: either 'a leak of 75 MB an hour is flagged within 2 hours 5 minutes' with the default min_slope left at 50MB/h, or lower the default threshold; state that MB in settings is 1024 x 1024 bytes.
findings.cost: One sentence in docs/01 and the gate
findings.decision_question: Raise the gate's leak rate above the threshold (75 MB/h), or lower the default threshold below the gate (e.g. 30MB/h, more false alarms)? Recommendation: keep the threshold and raise the gate rate, with 125 minutes.
findings.refutation_attempt: Re-ran with the decimal case added. Checked whether the detector is meant to run on a finer tier: docs/14 names minute buckets for the hourly check.
findings.related_prior_findings: R11, R34; lead reviewer's leads 10 and 33

findings.title: The 20 tests catch 1 of 29 deliberately broken behaviours
findings.evidence: uv run python docs/review/probes/e-baseline/mutation_check.py (copies src, tests and pyproject.toml to a temporary folder outside the repository; the control is caught): '28 of 29 broken behaviours survived'. Survivors include: I/O reported as running total not delta; rule priority ignored; a rule beats kernel-group membership; inherit_from_parent ignored; Submeter's own process not recognised; cmdline condition ignored; workload I/O and memory not summed; CPU pending at exit, at midnight rollover and at close thrown away; no keyframe after the first; WAL off; histograms not time-weighted; active seconds never counted; every bucket well covered; a process with unreadable I/O dropped; idle counted as busy; overrides lose to environment; layers applied in reverse; a default and a range differing from docs/08; minute retention ignored by choose_tier; every weekly file expired; core importing cli through a relative import. tests/test_layers.py:21-32 records only node.module, so 'from ..cli import app' is not seen.
findings.impact: AGENTS.md's 'a change in behaviour starts with a failing test' has nothing to start from for most promises in docs/14, so parallel builders can break them without any gate failing.
findings.proposed_change: tests/: add focused tests for each survivor above (about ten tests). tests/test_layers.py: resolve relative imports with node.level (three lines), which is the fix-now part.
findings.cost: Three lines for the layer test now; about ten tests as a planned task
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked that the copy's tests import the copy's code (pytest pythonpath=['src'] and the control mutation fails). Checked a sample of survivors against the tests: e.g. the two rule-priority tests list rules in priority order already, and no test has an exiting process.

findings.title: The layer table forbids the planned collector loop from importing the raw store
findings.evidence: tooling_cases.out.txt: 'collector/loop.py imports submeter.store.raw: exit 1; 1 failed'. tests/test_layers.py:9-18 puts collector, store and attribution all at layer 2 and line 43 requires a strictly lower layer. docs/14-baseline-modules.md: store.raw 'Imported by: Nothing yet. The collector loop will, in phase 1'; docs/17-build-prompt.md:269 'the collector loop ... around the existing sampler'.
findings.impact: The first phase-1 task fails the layer test, and each builder will edit the shared LAYER table and AGENTS.md's layer rule differently.
findings.proposed_change: Decide now where the loop and the server's writer loop live, e.g. a new package service at layer 3 beside cli, and add it to tests/test_layers.py LAYER and to the AGENTS.md rule.
findings.cost: Two lines in the test and one in AGENTS.md
findings.decision_question: Put the collector and server loops in (a) a new layer-3 package (service or daemon), or (b) move collector to layer 3? Recommendation: (a), so the sampler stays a pure layer-2 module.
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked whether the loop could avoid importing store and attribution: it must call the sampler, the attributor and the raw writer.

findings.title: One process with an unexpected read error aborts the whole snapshot, and zombies are dropped with readable CPU
findings.evidence: provider_cases.out.txt (psutil patched): 'io_counters raises RuntimeError: _read lets it out (/proc/4242/io file was empty)'; 'io_counters raises OSError: _read lets it out ([Errno 31] device failure)'. psutil _pslinux.py:1808-1825 raises RuntimeError for an empty io file and ValueError for a missing field; psutil_provider.py:76-82 catches only AccessDenied and NotImplementedError. Zombie: 'psutil still reads its CPU time (0.35 s); present in the provider's snapshot: False' (psutil_provider.py:102-103 catches ZombieProcess with NoSuchProcess and returns None).
findings.impact: A single malformed /proc entry costs the whole tick (or crashes the collector if the loop does not catch it), against 'never dropped'. Exited-but-unreaped children are the short-lived processes polling most needs, and their final CPU is thrown away.
findings.proposed_change: providers/psutil_provider.py: each optional read catches psutil.Error, OSError, RuntimeError and ValueError and leaves that field None; ZombieProcess on cmdline or cwd keeps the record with its CPU.
findings.cost: About 10 lines and one test
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked whether psutil's wrap_exceptions converts these: it converts only PermissionError, ProcessLookupError and FileNotFoundError (_pslinux.py:1584-1607). Trigger frequency of an empty io file is not measured; the escape path is certain.

findings.title: Per-process CPU carried in memory is lost on a crash, up to the keyframe interval, against '5 seconds'
findings.evidence: raw_store_cases.out.txt (300 processes at 0.4% of a core, killed 9 minutes after a keyframe): 'processes used 648.0 CPU-s over 540 s; process_raw holds 1.2 in 300 rows; workload_raw holds 648.0'. raw.py:134-145 writes a row only when pending reaches cpu_points of the waited time, on a memory move, or at a keyframe; config.py:64-66 allows a keyframe interval up to 1h. docs/17-build-prompt.md:138: 'A crash or power loss may lose up to 5 seconds of samples'.
findings.impact: Per-process history loses up to 10 minutes (default) of CPU on any crash, and in normal running places quiet processes' CPU up to 10 minutes late, which can move it into the wrong hour for the hourly top-ten executables (R28).
findings.proposed_change: store/raw.py:138: also write when waited reaches a maximum carry (e.g. 60 s) and at each hour boundary; or state in docs/06 that per-process rows can lose up to one keyframe interval.
findings.cost: Two lines and a test
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked whether workload rows carry the loss: they do not (648.0 stored). The keyframe path flushes pending CPU (control case 4: used 1.699, stored 1.699).

findings.title: Settings validation has holes: unknown alert metrics, threshold names, unselected profiles, negative or NaN values, and uncaught file errors
findings.evidence: config_cases.out.txt: "metric 'cpu_coress' on workload 'agent:*': accepted"; "metric 'commit_fraction' on workload 'browser': accepted"; 'verdict.thresholds.cpu_tyme = 0.85: accepted'; 'bad values in a profile, no profile selected: accepted'; 'profile = 5, profile selected: CRASH TypeError'; '[storage.retention] raw = -5: accepted', 'raw = nan: accepted', 'disk_budget = -1: accepted', 'min_slope = -1: accepted', 'cooldown = -60: accepted', 'unattributed_alert = "250%": accepted'. cli_cases.out.txt: 'config check MISSING: exit code 1, uncaught FileNotFoundError'; 'config show --file MISSING: exit code 0' (cli.py:47 silently uses defaults); 'top --rules with an unknown key: exit code 1, uncaught ValidationError'; 'config check on a UTF-16 file: uncaught UnicodeDecodeError'. docs/08-configuration.md:130: 'A rule that names any other metric is refused when the settings are loaded'. config.py:143,153,293-299,97-99.
findings.impact: A typo in an alert or threshold silently does nothing; a bad laptop profile passes config check and fails at run time; retention.raw = -5 makes FileMap.expired_raw list yesterday's raw file right after midnight, before it is rolled up.
findings.proposed_change: core/config.py: AlertRule.metric as a Literal of the seven ids in docs/08 with the applies-to check; Verdict.thresholds as a model; validate every profile at load; a non-negative, finite range for every Duration, Size, Rate and Fraction (unattributed_alert 0 to 100%). cli.py: a named --file or --rules that does not exist, does not decode or does not validate exits 2 with one line per problem.
findings.cost: About 40 lines and two tests
findings.refutation_attempt: docs/14 says 'every default and range in the tables of docs/08 was checked': the retention, budget and analysis rows have no range there, which is why nothing refuses them. Checked docs/08 for ranges on these: none given.

findings.title: choose_tier can answer from a tier that was already deleted
findings.evidence: interface_cases.out.txt: 'retention.raw = 60d (docs/08: keep full detail longer), minute = 30d; a 12-hour window 45 days back is answered from the minute tier, which was deleted 15 days earlier'. query.py:40-50: the point budget moves to the next tier without checking that its retention covers the window.
findings.impact: With raw retention raised as docs/08 suggests, history queries 30 to 60 days back return empty minute data although raw data exists.
findings.proposed_change: store/query.py: skip tiers whose retention does not cover the window start; if only raw does, return raw with a wider step.
findings.cost: About 5 lines and a test
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked config for a rule that raw retention may not exceed minute retention: none.

findings.title: histogram.percentile(q=100) returns the top of the scale (256 cores) for about a quarter of buckets
findings.evidence: rollup_cases.out.txt: '2000 minute buckets of values between 0.5 and 4 cores: 469 report a maximum of 256 cores'; controls q=99, 99.9, 99.999 give 4.11 to 4.14. histogram.py:77 total = sum(counts), compared with a running += total in the loop; when rounding leaves running below target the loop ends and line 92 returns scale.high. Also 'steady memory 1 MiB: p50=8.0 MiB' and '15 MiB: p50=8.0 MiB', 'cores 0.002: p50=0.0050' (the underflow bin is read by interpolation).
findings.impact: Any caller asking for the maximum from merged bins gets 256 cores or 256 GiB. Idle workloads and small processes read the same fixed values whatever their real level.
findings.proposed_change: core/histogram.py percentile: when the loop ends, return the upper edge of the last non-empty bin (or compare with a relative tolerance); docs/14: state that values below the scale read as half its low edge.
findings.cost: Two lines
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked whether q=100 is used: no caller yet, but nothing refuses it and a maximum is the natural request.

findings.title: A wall clock stepped back is not a gap and timestamps go backwards; a step forward discards a real interval
findings.evidence: sampler_cases.out.txt case 5: 'forward 5 s: gap=True, interval_s=6, used 0.8 CPU-s, credited 0'; 'back 5 s: gap=False, interval_s=1, taken_at went from 1006 to 1002, credited 0.8'. sampler.py:55 treats wall minus monotonic beyond 2 s as a gap and ignores the other sign; raw.py:103,113 INSERT OR REPLACE keyed on ts; RawStore.write picks the file by utc_day(taken_at) (raw.py:265-274).
findings.impact: After a backward step, rows are stored out of order and can land in the previous day's file and the wrong buckets; after a forward NTP correction, an observed interval is thrown away as a gap.
findings.proposed_change: collector/sampler.py: derive taken_at from a monotonic anchor (anchor wall time + monotonic elapsed), re-anchor on a step and record it as an event (an epoch change), not a gap.
findings.cost: About 8 lines
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked docs/17 'Detect suspend and resume': it covers suspend, not clock steps.

findings.title: Data folders and files are readable by other local users
findings.evidence: uv run python docs/review/probes/e-baseline/file_modes.py (umask 002): 'data folder drwxrwxr-x', 'raw folder drwxrwxr-x', 'raw file -rw-r--r--', 'raw write-ahead log -rw-r--r--', 'state folder drwxrwxr-x', 'lock file -rw-------', 'pid file -rw-rw-r--'. files.py:109-119 mkdir with default mode; raw.py:66-68 sqlite3.connect creates with default mode. docs/17-build-prompt.md: 'Restrict every data file and the API token to the current user.'
findings.impact: On Linux, any local account that can traverse the home folder can read process names, workloads and redacted command lines.
findings.proposed_change: store/files.py ensure: mkdir with mode 0o700 and chmod existing folders; store/raw.py: create the database file with 0o600 before sqlite opens it.
findings.cost: About 6 lines and a test (POSIX only)
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked the token path: not built yet. Windows %LOCALAPPDATA% is per-user by default, so this is Linux only.

findings.title: The records in core/models.py cannot express most of what the brief adds next, and every builder will edit that one file
findings.evidence: interface_cases.out.txt: '10 of 14 catalogue rows have no field in Bucket' (no fields for USS/PSS with age, threads and handles, GPU, VRAM, connections, per-core load and frequency, commit and paging, run queue and PSI, disk latency, Submeter's own cost); "Availability('opaque'), as docs/03 prints for vm.guest: refused" (docs/03-cli-output.md:61). models.py:131 SampleBatch keeps one summed cpu_busy_s although docs/06-storage.md:91 keeps load per core in the raw and minute tiers; WorkloadSample has no epoch and no gap flag; ProcessCounters has no child CPU, handles or second memory unit.
findings.impact: Each later component must change the same frozen records and the raw schema, so parallel builders will conflict in one shared file and each migration touches raw files already on disk.
findings.proposed_change: Before the build: one pass over core/models.py and store/raw.py adding the docs/06 catalogue fields as Optional (None = unavailable), an epoch on WorkloadSample, per-core busy in SampleBatch, OPAQUE in Availability, and a raw schema_version 2; or split models.py by area so builders do not share one file.
findings.cost: About 60 lines of fields as one planned task before parallel work starts
findings.refutation_attempt: docs/14 says the records are 'the contract between the collector, the server and the CLI', with no note that they are a first cut. Checked docs/13 for a component that owns schema growth: none.

findings.title: On Windows the system busy sum probably counts interrupt and DPC time twice
findings.evidence: psutil C per-CPU times (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/giampaolo/psutil/master/psutil/arch/windows/cpu.c): '// kernel time includes idle time on windows ... systemt = kernel - idle;' with interrupt and dpc returned as separate fields; _pswindows.py:270-276 returns (user, system, idle, interrupt, dpc). psutil_provider.py:115-122 computes busy as the sum of all fields minus idle, so interrupt and dpc are added on top of system. Whether KernelTime already contains them is not stated in any Microsoft page found. On Linux the same formula is right: provider_cases.out.txt 'every core's fields (guest taken out) add up to the 2.00 s elapsed within 0.05 s'.
findings.impact: Machine busy time, and so the System bucket and reconciliation, would be overstated by the interrupt and DPC share on Windows.
findings.proposed_change: providers/psutil_provider.py: compute busy per core as elapsed minus idle where the fields do not partition time, and add the partition check to scripts/platform_check.py.
findings.cost: A few lines plus one platform check
findings.refutation_attempt: Searched for vendor documentation on SYSTEM_PROCESSOR_PERFORMANCE_INFORMATION.KernelTime contents: only third-party sources, which disagree.
findings.would_confirm: On Windows: uv run python -c "import psutil,time;a=psutil.cpu_times(percpu=True);time.sleep(10);b=psutil.cpu_times(percpu=True);print([round(sum(y)-sum(x),2) for x,y in zip(a,b)])". Values near 10 mean the fields partition time; values above 10 by about interrupt+dpc confirm the double count

findings.title: Windows lock and pid file: a restart right after a crash may be refused, and holder() reports a dead pid
findings.evidence: LockFileEx remarks (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-lockfileex): 'If a process terminates with a portion of a file locked ... the locks are unlocked by the operating system. However, the time it takes for the operating system to unlock these locks depends upon available system resources.' files.py:219-231 tries once with LK_NBLCK and returns False. lock_cases.out.txt (Linux, verified): 'after the holder is killed: holder() still returns its pid: True; a process with that pid exists: False'; files.py:233-238.
findings.impact: A collector restarted by a scheduled task right after a crash may exit with 'another copy is already running'; doctor could name a dead or reused pid as the running collector.
findings.proposed_change: store/files.py: acquire retries for a few seconds before giving up; holder() returns None when a non-blocking try-lock succeeds.
findings.cost: About 8 lines
findings.refutation_attempt: platform_check.py kills the holder and retries after 0.5 s, which is the case to watch on Windows; it has not run there.
findings.would_confirm: On Windows: uv run python scripts/platform_check.py several times in a row and watch 'free after the holder was killed'; and a loop that kills a holder process and immediately calls InstanceLock(path).acquire() 100 times, counting refusals

findings.title: Private bytes depend on a psutil alias that psutil 8 deprecates, with a silent fallback to working set
findings.evidence: psutil_provider.py:63 int(getattr(memory, 'private', memory.rss)). psutil 7.2.2 (uv.lock) has 'private' in the Windows pmem (_ntuples.py:242-256) and fills it even for protected processes via the NtQuerySystemInformation fallback (_pswindows.py:789-811). psutil.io/api (8.x): vms 'On Windows maps to PrivateUsage (private committed pages only), which differs from the UNIX definition;'; an earlier fetch of the same page quoted the 8.0.0 note 'pagefile and private -> vms' and 'All these old names still work but raise DeprecationWarning.' pyproject.toml pins psutil>=6.0 with no upper bound.
findings.impact: An upgrade past the alias's removal would switch Windows memory to working set without an error, which is the R06 problem leak detection was designed to avoid.
findings.proposed_change: providers/psutil_provider.py: read the field explicitly by platform and psutil version (private on 7.x, vms on 8.x) and raise if neither exists; or pin psutil<8 in pyproject.toml until tested.
findings.cost: Three lines
findings.refutation_attempt: Checked uv.lock: 7.2.2, so today's build is correct; the risk is the next relock.

findings.title: The standard checks do not type-check Windows-only code on Linux, and ruff format checks Markdown
findings.evidence: tooling_cases.out.txt: mypy on a win32-guarded bad return 'as run here: exit 0; Success' and 'with --platform win32: exit 1'. AGENTS.md 'Checks' lists only 'uv run mypy src tests' although docs/14:11 says mypy was 'checked as Linux and again as Windows' (both pass today: mypy --platform win32 src tests, 25 files, no issues). tooling_cases.out.txt: 'ruff format --check on a folder holding only note.md: exit 1; 1 file would be reformatted' (ruff 0.17.6 formats Python blocks in Markdown); ground ruff-format counted 25 Markdown files. version_gate.out.txt: Python 3.14.5 runs the checks (no .python-version); ruff with target py312 flags both 3.14-only constructs tried ('exit 1' each), so the unpinned interpreter is a lesser risk.
findings.impact: Windows-only providers and the launcher written on Linux pass the local gate and fail only in Windows CI; a document with an unformatted Python block fails the format gate, and running the fixer rewrites the brief.
findings.proposed_change: AGENTS.md Checks: add 'uv run mypy --platform win32 src tests'. pyproject.toml [tool.ruff]: exclude docs/ from formatting (or extend-exclude = ['*.md']). Optionally add .python-version 3.12 so local runs match the brief.
findings.cost: Three lines
findings.refutation_attempt: Ran mypy both ways on src and tests: both clean today, so this is a gate gap, not a present defect.

measurements: Mutation (temp copy, 20 tests): control caught; 28 of 29 broken behaviours survived. Sampler: restricted->readable flip credits 5000 CPU-s in 1 s; hot/cold 20 s: cold used 2.40 CPU-s credited 0.00, 60 false exits and 60 false starts; gap rule: 40/50/60 s intervals all gap=True; top --seconds 31 -> 0.000 CPU-s (2 s -> 3.510). Rollup across 1 h sleep: minute bucket covered_s 3601 of 60; 3 h merge covered 10800 for 7200 awake, mean 1.33 cores vs 2.00, p50 1.951, p25 0.007. Histogram q=100: 469 of 2000 buckets return 256 cores. Raw kill 9 min after keyframe: process_raw 1.2 of 648.0 CPU-s. Provider on this Linux machine: 457 processes, 299 restricted, all 299 for I/O only, 187 of them with CPU > 0, 77662 CPU-s held. Memory sum RSS/PSS: all own processes 11327/6659 MiB (x1.70), chrome x1.95, claude x1.40, Web Content x5.14. Children time: seen 0.42 + parent child-time 0.42 = 0.84 for 0.42 used; orphaned grandchild 0.31 CPU-s, parent child time +0.05. Start time: btime-based vs clock-derived boot differs by 0.925 s. Leak check: 50 MiB/h with noise 9/20 within 125 min; 50,000,000 B/h 0/20 ever; 55 MiB/h 20/20. File modes (umask 002): data dirs 0775, raw file and WAL 0644, pid file 0664, lock 0600. mypy strict: 25 files clean as linux and as win32.
nothing_found: Sampler pid reuse and first sighting: a new start time is a new process, an older first sighting is credited 0, one born in the interval gets all its CPU (sampler_cases case 6).

psutil process_iter cache and pid reuse: the provider's ppid() call runs psutil's is_running() check (psutil/__init__.py:459-469, 625-650), so a reused pid is dropped for one snapshot, not given the old process's key.
Linux system busy sum: fields minus guest add to the elapsed time within 0.05 s (provider_cases case 5).

Attribution cycles and ties: a parent cycle ends in Unattributed, equal CPU keeps first-seen order (attribution_cases case 5). Deep chains fail only past about 1000 levels (RecursionError at 1500 children-first), which real machines do not produce.
Raw store exact sums through exit, UTC midnight rollover and keyframes: used 1.699, stored 1.699; keyframes at 0 and 600 s from midnight in the new file (raw_store_cases case 4).
Instance lock on Linux: a second holder is refused, the lock is free after the holder is killed, the pid file goes on clean release (lock_cases).
mypy strict on src and tests passes both as Linux and with --platform win32 (25 files).

Python version: ruff with target py312 flags a PEP 649 forward name and PEP 758 unparenthesised except, which Python 3.14 accepts and 3.12 rejects (version_gate), so the unpinned 3.14.5 does not hide those.
Probe folder passes ruff check and ruff format --check (16 files).
